review_notes:
I read the whole file and checked how the `cuspIntegral` lemmas are used elsewhere in the repo. The file has two simp lemmas, `cuspIntegral_same` and `cuspIntegral_zero`. Both are unconditional, have strictly simpler right-hand sides, and cannot loop.

`cuspIntegral_symm` is correctly not simp, because it would rewrite `cuspIntegral F b a` to a negation of `cuspIntegral F a b` and then rewrite back. `cuspIntegral_slash` is also not simp. Its right-hand side moves the action onto the cusps, so a simp orientation would be a design choice rather than a clear normal form. `cuspIntegral_add` and `cuspIntegral_sum` carry integrability hypotheses, so they are poor simp lemmas.

`cuspIntegral_smul` is unconditional and would be a plausible simp lemma. However, its downstream uses all state it explicitly, in `rw` chains (Pairing.lean lines 77, 150) or as a term (Integral.lean line 401). I found no use where its absence from the simp set forces a workaround, so I did not report it. The same applies to `cuspIntegral_smul_zero_smul_infty`, which needs a side condition `hg` and a particular argument shape.

I found no competing rules and no unwanted unfolding. The private lemmas have no simp attributes. I could not run Lean, so I made no claims about simp behaviour or failures.
